simple: many computers connected by a network and managed together so that they can share work.
analogy: the seven friends along the railway line, with one organiser.
precise: a set of independent computers (nodes), usually alike and connected by a local network, that is operated as one system: one administrative domain, a common view of users and storage, and a scheduler that decides where work runs.
source: D2 of F5-22 (Maarten van Steen, Andrew S. Tanenbaum, "Distributed Systems" (edition to be recorded), the sections on cluster computing systems (tier 3; guide 4.5)); D1 of F5-22 (SchedMD, Slurm documentation: "Quick Start User Guide" and "Quick Start Administrator Guide" (architecture overview: controller, node daemons, login and compute nodes, partitions, jobs) (tier 2; guide 4.5)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: one computer in a cluster.
analogy: one friend's house, with that friend's own tools.
precise: one machine with its own processors, memory, operating system and network interfaces; it fails independently of the others. Not the same as a circuit node (HW101) or a graph node.
source: D2 of F5-22 (Maarten van Steen, Andrew S. Tanenbaum, "Distributed Systems" (edition to be recorded), the sections on cluster computing systems (tier 3; guide 4.5)); D3 of F5-22 (Martin Kleppmann, "Designing Data-Intensive Applications", chapter 1 (reliability, hardware faults) and chapter 8 ("The Trouble with Distributed Systems") (tier 3; guide 4.5)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the login node is where people sign in and prepare work; compute nodes are where the work really runs.
analogy: the station where friends meet Lucía, and the houses where the chores happen.
precise: roles a cluster gives its nodes: users connect to a login (front-end) node, submit jobs to the scheduler, and the scheduler starts them on compute nodes; management services (the scheduler's controller, databases, monitoring) often run on separate management nodes.
source: D1 of F5-22 (SchedMD, Slurm documentation: "Quick Start User Guide" and "Quick Start Administrator Guide" (architecture overview: controller, node daemons, login and compute nodes, partitions, jobs) (tier 2; guide 4.5)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a piece of work you hand to the cluster that starts, runs and ends.
analogy: one chore card in Lucía's box.
precise: a request for resources (nodes, CPUs, memory, GPUs, a time limit) together with the program to run in them; it waits in a queue, is allocated resources, runs to completion or failure, and releases them.
source: D1 of F5-22 (SchedMD, Slurm documentation: "Quick Start User Guide" and "Quick Start Administrator Guide" (architecture overview: controller, node daemons, login and compute nodes, partitions, jobs) (tier 2; guide 4.5)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the program that decides which work runs where and when.
analogy: lucía, the organiser who assigns chores (registered mapping).
precise: software that tracks the resources of every node, keeps a queue of requests, chooses an allocation for each according to a policy (priorities, fairness, limits), starts the work on the chosen nodes and reclaims the resources when it ends. Not the same as the operating system's CPU scheduler of F3-03, which chooses among threads on one machine.
source: D1 of F5-22 (SchedMD, Slurm documentation: "Quick Start User Guide" and "Quick Start Administrator Guide" (architecture overview: controller, node daemons, login and compute nodes, partitions, jobs) (tier 2; guide 4.5)); D5 of F5-22 (Abhishek Verma, Luis Pedrosa, Madhukar Korupolu, David Oppenheimer, Eric Tune, John Wilkes, "Large-scale cluster management at Google with Borg", EuroSys 2015 (tier 5; guide 4.5)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a disk that every node can see, so a job finds its files on whichever node it lands.
analogy: the library all the towns can borrow from by post.
precise: a network file system mounted at the same path on the login and compute nodes, holding home directories, inputs and outputs; it is itself a distributed system that can be slow or fail (DS402).
source: D1 of F5-22 (SchedMD, Slurm documentation: "Quick Start User Guide" and "Quick Start Administrator Guide" (architecture overview: controller, node daemons, login and compute nodes, partitions, jobs) (tier 2; guide 4.5)); D3 of F5-22 (Martin Kleppmann, "Designing Data-Intensive Applications", chapter 1 (reliability, hardware faults) and chapter 8 ("The Trouble with Distributed Systems") (tier 3; guide 4.5)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a job whose parts must all keep running and keep talking; if one part stops, the whole job stops.
analogy: the library chore that needs three friends in the room all day.
precise: a parallel job whose processes exchange data during the run (for example with MPI collectives), so that progress needs every process; contrast with independent tasks that can each succeed or fail alone.
source: D4 of F5-22 (MPI Forum, "MPI: A Message-Passing Interface Standard" (version to be recorded): MPI_Init, MPI_Comm_rank, MPI_Comm_size, MPI_Get_processor_name, MPI_Wtime, MPI_Reduce, MPI_Finalize (tier 1; guide 3.1)); D3 of F5-22 (Martin Kleppmann, "Designing Data-Intensive Applications", chapter 1 (reliability, hardware faults) and chapter 8 ("The Trouble with Distributed Systems") (tier 3; guide 4.5)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the number of one process in a parallel job, counted from zero.
analogy: the badge number each friend wears for one chore.
precise: the integer identifying a process within an MPI communicator; with N processes in MPI_COMM_WORLD the ranks are 0 to N − 1, returned by MPI_Comm_rank.
source: D4 of F5-22 (MPI Forum, "MPI: A Message-Passing Interface Standard" (version to be recorded): MPI_Init, MPI_Comm_rank, MPI_Comm_size, MPI_Get_processor_name, MPI_Wtime, MPI_Reduce, MPI_Finalize (tier 1; guide 3.1)); R3 of F5-22 (lab run of Listing 3 by run.sh: F5-22/pi_mpi.out, pi_mpi.log (Open MPI 4.1.6 with g++ 13.3.0; one container with 4 logical CPUs; exit code 0)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a saved copy of a job's progress, so that after a failure it can continue instead of starting again.
analogy: writing on the library wall which shelves are already sorted.
precise: application or system state written to stable storage at chosen points, from which a restarted job resumes; the cost of writing it is traded against the work lost per failure. Not the same as a file-system journal checkpoint (OS401).
source: D3 of F5-22 (Martin Kleppmann, "Designing Data-Intensive Applications", chapter 1 (reliability, hardware faults) and chapter 8 ("The Trouble with Distributed Systems") (tier 3; guide 4.5)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: you hand in work and go away; the cluster runs it when resources are free and keeps the result.
analogy: putting a chore card in Lucía's box instead of standing next to her.
precise: non-interactive execution of jobs from a queue: each job declares its resource needs and time limit at submission, waits until the scheduler allocates them, runs without user interaction, and writes its output to files.
source: D1 of F5-23 (SchedMD, Slurm documentation: "Quick Start User Guide", "Quick Start Administrator Guide", and the man pages of sbatch, srun, squeue and sinfo (tier 2; guide 4.5)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a shell script whose top lines tell the scheduler what the job needs.
analogy: the chore card, tools list on top, steps below.
precise: a script submitted to the batch system; scheduler directives in special comment lines (for Slurm, lines beginning #SBATCH) set resources and options, and the rest of the script runs on the first allocated node when the job starts. To the shell, the directive lines are ordinary comments (R3).
source: D1 of F5-23 (SchedMD, Slurm documentation: "Quick Start User Guide", "Quick Start Administrator Guide", and the man pages of sbatch, srun, squeue and sinfo (tier 2; guide 4.5)); R3 of F5-23 (lab run of Listing 2 with plain bash by run.sh: F5-23/job_bash.out, job_bash.log (GNU bash 5.2.21, exit code 0; untested under Slurm)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a named group of nodes with its own rules, like a separate queue.
analogy: the river towns and the mountain towns, each with its own list.
precise: Slurm's grouping of nodes into job queues, each with limits (for example maximum time, allowed users) and its own priority; a job is submitted to one or more partitions.
source: D1 of F5-23 (SchedMD, Slurm documentation: "Quick Start User Guide", "Quick Start Administrator Guide", and the man pages of sbatch, srun, squeue and sinfo (tier 2; guide 4.5)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the longest your job may run; when it is reached, the job is stopped.
analogy: "until 6 p.m." on the chore card.
precise: a wall-clock limit declared at submission; the scheduler uses it to plan (reservations and backfill) and enforces it by terminating the job when it expires.
source: D1 of F5-23 (SchedMD, Slurm documentation: "Quick Start User Guide", "Quick Start Administrator Guide", and the man pages of sbatch, srun, squeue and sinfo (tier 2; guide 4.5)); R1 of F5-23 (lab run of Listing 1: F5-23/batchsim.out, batchsim.log (g++ 13.3.0, ASan and UBSan, exit code 0)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a number that decides which waiting job is considered first.
analogy: lucía's "urgent first, then oldest".
precise: a value computed per pending job by the scheduler's priority policy; Slurm's multifactor priority combines weighted factors such as age, fair share, job size, partition and quality of service.
source: D2 of F5-23 (SchedMD, Slurm documentation: "Multifactor Priority Plugin" (tier 2)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the first job in the queue cannot start, and everything behind it waits too.
analogy: the crane card at the front of the box.
precise: in a strictly ordered queue, a job that cannot be scheduled prevents the scheduling of lower-priority jobs that could run; backfill and feasibility checks are the two remedies.
source: R1 of F5-23 (lab run of Listing 1: F5-23/batchsim.out, batchsim.log (g++ 13.3.0, ASan and UBSan, exit code 0)); R2 of F5-23 (lab run of Listing 1 on pending.in by run.sh: F5-23/pending.out, pending.log (same toolchain and flags, exit code 0))

simple: letting a smaller job jump ahead when it will not delay the jobs in front of it.
analogy: yusuf's one-hour chore before noon.
precise: a policy that, when the highest-priority pending job cannot start, computes the earliest time it can (a reservation, assuming running jobs end at their time limits) and starts lower-priority jobs now only if they fit and do not delay that reservation, because they end before it or use nodes it does not need.
source: D3 of F5-23 (SchedMD, Slurm documentation: "Scheduling Configuration Guide" (main and backfill scheduling) (tier 2)); R1 of F5-23 (lab run of Listing 1: F5-23/batchsim.out, batchsim.log (g++ 13.3.0, ASan and UBSan, exit code 0)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the scheduler's short note saying why a job is still waiting.
analogy: lucía's "not yet" or "never" written on the card.
precise: a code the scheduler attaches to each pending job (for example "resources" or "priority" in this chapter's simulator; Slurm's own reason names are in the unverified box of Layer 3); the first thing to read when a job does not start.
source: D1 of F5-23 (SchedMD, Slurm documentation: "Quick Start User Guide", "Quick Start Administrator Guide", and the man pages of sbatch, srun, squeue and sinfo (tier 2; guide 4.5)); R2 of F5-23 (lab run of Listing 1 on pending.in by run.sh: F5-23/pending.out, pending.log (same toolchain and flags, exit code 0)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: one launch of a program inside a job's allocation; a job can have several.
analogy: the separate steps on one chore card, done by the same friends.
precise: a set of tasks launched within an existing allocation (in Slurm by srun inside the job); steps can run one after another or side by side, sharing the job's resources.
source: D1 of F5-23 (SchedMD, Slurm documentation: "Quick Start User Guide", "Quick Start Administrator Guide", and the man pages of sbatch, srun, squeue and sinfo (tier 2; guide 4.5)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a group of ordinary programs that the operating system keeps in their own little world, with their own files and limits.
analogy: a sealed chore kit used in a spare room with its own door, number plate and water rule.
precise: one or more processes running on the host kernel inside a set of namespaces (their own view of process ids, host name, mounts, network and more), confined by control groups (resource limits and accounting) and by privilege restrictions, with a root file system taken from a container image. Not the same as a C++ container such as std::vector (SP101).
source: D1 of F5-24 (Open Container Initiative, "OCI Runtime Specification" (the version runc reports, 1.3.0, to be confirmed in the document): configuration, Linux-specific configuration, lifecycle and operations (tier 1)); D3 of F5-24 (Linux man-pages project: namespaces(7), pid_namespaces(7), user_namespaces(7), unshare(2), capabilities(7) (tier 2)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a separate copy of one thing the system usually shares, such as the list of process numbers or the computer's name.
analogy: the room's own number plate: the same house, a different address inside.
precise: a kernel feature that wraps a global resource so that processes inside the namespace see their own isolated instance of it; Linux has namespaces for mounts, UTS (host and domain name), IPC, PIDs, networks, users, control groups and time. Not the same as an NVMe namespace (DR301) or a C++ namespace.
source: D3 of F5-24 (Linux man-pages project: namespaces(7), pid_namespaces(7), user_namespaces(7), unshare(2), capabilities(7) (tier 2)); L1 of F5-24 (Local headers opened in this build (libc6-dev 2.39-0ubuntu8.9): /usr/include/x86_64-linux-gnu/bits/sched.h (lines 55–77 define CLONE_NEWNS, CLONE_NEWCGROUP, CLONE_NEWUTS, CLONE_NEWIPC, CLONE_NEWUSER, CLONE_NEWPID, CLONE_NEWNET, CLONE_NEWTIME) and bits/signum-generic.h (line 53 SIGTERM 15, line 59 SIGKILL 9) (tier 4: what this C library defines)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a group of processes that the kernel measures and limits together.
analogy: "this room may use at most two buckets of water".
precise: a kernel mechanism that organises processes in a hierarchy and lets controllers (memory, CPU, PIDs, I/O, devices and others) account for and limit their resource use; Linux has two versions, v1 (one hierarchy per controller) and v2 (one unified hierarchy).
source: D4 of F5-24 (The Linux kernel documentation: "Control Groups" (cgroup v1), "Memory Resource Controller" (cgroup v1 memory), and "Control Group v2" (tier 2)); R5 of F5-24 (the memory runs: F5-24/oom_host.out (exit 0), oom_container.out (exit 137), container_limit.out (exit 0), oom_cgroup.out (exit 137, kernel counters), and their logs; Linux 6.18.44 cgroup v1 memory controller) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the packed contents of a container: its files and the settings to start it.
analogy: the sealed box before anyone opens it.
precise: an immutable bundle of file-system layers plus a configuration (default command, environment, and more), identified by a digest of its content and distributed through registries; the OCI Image Format Specification standardises it.
source: D2 of F5-24 (Open Container Initiative, "OCI Image Format Specification": layers, image configuration, manifest, content descriptors and digests (tier 1)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a folder that a container runtime can start: the files, plus a description of how to run them.
analogy: the opened kit laid out on the table with its instruction card.
precise: a directory with a root file system and a config.json describing the process, mounts, namespaces, resources and security settings, as defined by the OCI Runtime Specification; runc spec writes a default one (R3).
source: D1 of F5-24 (Open Container Initiative, "OCI Runtime Specification" (the version runc reports, 1.3.0, to be confirmed in the document): configuration, Linux-specific configuration, lifecycle and operations (tier 1)); R3 of F5-24 (runc spec summarised by Listing 3: F5-24/runc_spec.out, runc_spec.log) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the program that actually creates a container from a bundle and starts its first process.
analogy: the friend who opens the kit in the spare room and fits the door rules.
precise: a program implementing the OCI Runtime Specification's operations (create, start, kill, delete, state) by making the system calls that set up namespaces, control groups, mounts and privileges; runc is the reference implementation, and higher-level tools (container engines, Kubernetes' kubelet in F5-25) call such a runtime.
source: D1 of F5-24 (Open Container Initiative, "OCI Runtime Specification" (the version runc reports, 1.3.0, to be confirmed in the document): configuration, Linux-specific configuration, lifecycle and operations (tier 1)); R2 of F5-24 (runc --help, COMMANDS section: F5-24/runc_help.out, runc_help.log (runc 1.5.1, spec 1.3.0)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the kernel stopping a program at once because its group used all the memory it was allowed.
analogy: the tap shut on the third bucket.
precise: when a memory control group reaches its limit and the kernel cannot reclaim enough memory from it, the kernel's out-of-memory handler kills a process in that group with SIGKILL; the parent sees termination by signal 9, which a shell reports as exit status 137 (128 + 9).
source: D4 of F5-24 (The Linux kernel documentation: "Control Groups" (cgroup v1), "Memory Resource Controller" (cgroup v1 memory), and "Control Group v2" (tier 2)); D5 of F5-24 (Free Software Foundation, "Bash Reference Manual", section "Exit Status" (status 128 + n for a command ended by signal n) (tier 2)); R5 of F5-24 (the memory runs: F5-24/oom_host.out (exit 0), oom_container.out (exit 137), container_limit.out (exit 0), oom_cgroup.out (exit 137, kernel counters), and their logs; Linux 6.18.44 cgroup v1 memory controller) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: one small piece of the administrator's power that can be given or taken away on its own.
analogy: one key from the house owner's ring, instead of the whole ring.
precise: Linux divides the privileges of the root user into named capabilities (for example CAP_KILL, CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE) that a process may hold or lack individually; container runtimes drop most of them, so root inside a container is weaker than root on the host.
source: D3 of F5-24 (Linux man-pages project: namespaces(7), pid_namespaces(7), user_namespaces(7), unshare(2), capabilities(7) (tier 2)); R3 of F5-24 (runc spec summarised by Listing 3: F5-24/runc_spec.out, runc_spec.log) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a system that keeps a set of containers running on a group of machines, the way you described you want them.
analogy: the noticeboard and its helpers.
precise: an open-source container orchestration system: users declare objects (desired state) through an API; control loops continuously drive the cluster's actual state toward it, scheduling containers onto nodes, replacing failed ones and routing traffic to them.
source: D1 of F5-25 (The Kubernetes project (CNCF), Kubernetes documentation: "Kubernetes Components" and "Cluster Architecture" (tier 2; guide 4.5)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the part of the cluster that decides and remembers; the nodes do the work.
analogy: the noticeboard with Rafael, Mei and Ingrid.
precise: the components that hold cluster state and make global decisions: the API server, its backing key-value store, the scheduler and the controller managers; they may run on dedicated machines and are replicated for availability.
source: D1 of F5-25 (The Kubernetes project (CNCF), Kubernetes documentation: "Kubernetes Components" and "Cluster Architecture" (tier 2; guide 4.5)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the one front door to the cluster's records; everyone reads and writes through it.
analogy: the noticeboard itself, with its rules about who may pin what.
precise: the component that exposes the Kubernetes API, validates and stores objects in the key-value store, and lets clients watch for changes; the other components communicate through it rather than with each other.
source: D1 of F5-25 (The Kubernetes project (CNCF), Kubernetes documentation: "Kubernetes Components" and "Cluster Architecture" (tier 2; guide 4.5)); D2 of F5-25 (Kubernetes documentation: "Kubernetes API Concepts" (watches, resource versions, optimistic concurrency) (tier 2)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the database where the cluster's records are kept safely on several machines.
analogy: the noticeboard's copies, kept identical in several town halls.
precise: a distributed, strongly consistent key-value store that replicates its data with the Raft consensus algorithm (DS302); Kubernetes uses it as the backing store for all cluster data.
source: D1 of F5-25 (The Kubernetes project (CNCF), Kubernetes documentation: "Kubernetes Components" and "Cluster Architecture" (tier 2; guide 4.5)); D6 of F5-25 (Diego Ongaro, John Ousterhout, "In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm (Extended Version)" (tier 5; guide 4.5; used in DS302), and the etcd project's documentation (tier 2) for etcd's use of Raft) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the smallest thing Kubernetes runs: one or a few containers that always go together.
analogy: one library branch, with its librarian and its book cart, always in the same town.
precise: a group of one or more containers scheduled together onto one node, sharing a network namespace (one IP address) and storage volumes; pods are disposable and are replaced, not repaired.
source: D3 of F5-25 (Kubernetes documentation: "Pods", "Deployments", "ReplicaSet", "Labels and Selectors", "StatefulSets" (tier 2)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a helper that keeps checking one kind of record and fixes any difference between what is wished and what is true.
analogy: rafael, who only counts libraries.
precise: a control loop that watches objects of some kinds through the API server, compares their desired state (spec) with the observed state (status), and acts through the API to reduce the difference; examples manage replica sets, deployments, nodes and endpoints.
source: D4 of F5-25 (Kubernetes documentation: "Controllers" (control loops, desired and current state) (tier 2)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: fixing things by looking at how they are now, not by remembering what happened.
analogy: rafael counts the libraries each time; he does not need to know there was a flood.
precise: a control style in which each loop iteration acts on the current difference between desired and observed state ("level"), not on individual change events ("edges"); a missed or duplicated event therefore does no lasting harm, because the next iteration sees the same difference.
source: D4 of F5-25 (Kubernetes documentation: "Controllers" (control loops, desired and current state) (tier 2)); R1 of F5-25 (lab run of Listing 1: F5-25/reconcile.out, reconcile.log (g++ 13.3.0, ASan and UBSan, exit code 0)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the agent on every node that starts the pods assigned to that node and reports on them.
analogy: the caretaker in each town.
precise: the node agent that watches for pods bound to its node, asks the container runtime to run their containers, reports pod and node status, and renews the node's heartbeat.
source: D1 of F5-25 (The Kubernetes project (CNCF), Kubernetes documentation: "Kubernetes Components" and "Cluster Architecture" (tier 2; guide 4.5)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: records that say "keep this many copies of this pod running", and how to change them gradually.
analogy: the wish "open in 3 towns", plus a plan for swapping old books for new ones town by town.
precise: a ReplicaSet keeps a stated number of pods matching a selector; a Deployment manages ReplicaSets to roll out a new pod template gradually and to roll back.
source: D3 of F5-25 (Kubernetes documentation: "Pods", "Deployments", "ReplicaSet", "Labels and Selectors", "StatefulSets" (tier 2)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: labels are name tags on objects; a selector is a rule like "everything tagged app=web".
analogy: coloured stickers on the library cards, and "all cards with a green sticker".
precise: labels are key–value pairs attached to objects; an equality-based selector matches an object when every key–value pair of the selector is present in the object's labels; controllers and services find their pods this way.
source: D3 of F5-25 (Kubernetes documentation: "Pods", "Deployments", "ReplicaSet", "Labels and Selectors", "StatefulSets" (tier 2)); R2 of F5-25 (lab run of Listing 2: F5-25/endpoints.out, endpoints.log (same toolchain, exit code 0)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: one stable name and address for a changing group of pods.
analogy: "the library", whichever towns it is open in today.
precise: an object that selects pods by labels and gives them a stable virtual address and name; the set of ready, selected pods' addresses (its endpoints) is kept up to date by a controller, and traffic to the service is spread over them.
source: D5 of F5-25 (Kubernetes documentation: "Service" and "Virtual IPs and Service Proxies" (tier 2)); R2 of F5-25 (lab run of Listing 2: F5-25/endpoints.out, endpoints.log (same toolchain, exit code 0)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the request is what a container is promised and what the scheduler counts; the limit is the most it may use.
analogy: "this library needs two shelves" (request) and "may never use more than three" (limit).
precise: per-container amounts of CPU and memory: the scheduler places pods by the sum of requests against a node's allocatable capacity; limits are enforced on the node through control groups (F5-24).
source: D7 of F5-25 (Kubernetes documentation: "Resource Management for Pods and Containers" (requests and limits) (tier 2)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: Slurm's way to count things on a node that are not CPUs or memory, such as GPUs.
analogy: the number of ovens in each kitchen, written on Lucía's list.
precise: a named, countable per-node resource (for example GPUs, optionally with a type) declared in Slurm's configuration and requested by jobs; Slurm allocates specific devices to the job and can restrict the job to them.
source: D1 of F5-26 (SchedMD, Slurm documentation: "Generic Resource (GRES) Scheduling", "sbatch" manual page, "Cgroups Guide" / cgroup.conf (tier 2; guide 4.5)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a helper program on each Kubernetes node that tells the cluster "this node has 8 GPUs" and connects a pod to the GPUs it was given.
analogy: the kitchen's caretaker, who counts the ovens and unlocks the ones assigned to you.
precise: a node-local component that registers with the kubelet, advertises a countable extended resource (for example GPUs of one vendor), and, when a pod is assigned devices, returns what the container needs to use them (device files, environment variables, mounts).
source: D2 of F5-26 (The Kubernetes project (CNCF), Kubernetes documentation: "Schedule GPUs", "Device Plugins" (tier 2)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: which GPUs a program can see and use; a job should see only the GPUs it was given.
analogy: only your assigned ovens are unlocked.
precise: the set of GPUs a process can open and enumerate, limited from outside by device access rules (control groups, container device lists) and, for CUDA programs, by the CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES environment variable, which restricts and renumbers the devices the CUDA runtime reports.
source: L1 of F5-26 (CUDA 12.0 headers in the build container (tier 4, opened): cuda.h line 240 (CUDA_VERSION 12000) and lines 4250–4251 (MIG UUID of "the subscribed MIG compute instance"); cuda_runtime_api.h lines 4936–4937 (CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES "is recommended to restrict CUDA to only use those GPUs that have peer-to-peer support") and 4946–4947 (environment variables "described in the CUDA programming guide"), line 1409 (cudaGetDeviceCount); driver_types.h line 545 (cudaErrorNoDevice = 100), lines 955–978 (MPS error codes)); D5 of F5-26 (NVIDIA, "CUDA C++ Programming Guide", section "CUDA Environment Variables" (tier 1), the section the local header refers to) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: free GPUs scattered over many nodes, so that a job needing many GPUs on one node cannot start although enough are free in total.
analogy: 24 free ovens, but never 8 in one kitchen.
precise: the state in which the free capacity of a cluster, summed over nodes, satisfies a request, but no set of nodes satisfies the request's per-node shape; it is caused by placement decisions and job sizes.
source: R1 of F5-26 (lab run of Listing 1 on gpupack.in: F5-26/gpupack.out, gpupack.log (g++ 13.3.0, ASan and UBSan, exit code 0))

simple: packing fills busy nodes first; spreading puts each job on the emptiest node.
analogy: tuesday's rule and Monday's rule.
precise: node-scoring rules: packing (best fit, most-allocated) chooses the feasible node with the least free capacity, keeping whole nodes free for large jobs; spreading (least-allocated) chooses the node with the most free capacity, balancing load and limiting what one node failure affects.
source: D6 of F5-26 (SchedMD, Slurm "Topology Guide"; Kubernetes documentation "Control Topology Management Policies on a node" and "Resource Bin Packing" (tier 2)); R1 of F5-26 (lab run of Listing 1 on gpupack.in: F5-26/gpupack.out, gpupack.log (g++ 13.3.0, ASan and UBSan, exit code 0)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how the GPUs inside a node are connected; some pairs talk much faster than others.
analogy: ovens on the same bench pass trays directly.
precise: the interconnect graph of a node's GPUs, network adapters and CPU sockets (direct GPU links, PCIe switches, CPU root complexes); a group of GPUs joined by the fast links is called an island in this chapter; placing a job's GPUs inside one island, near its CPU and network adapter, speeds its communication (DG401).
source: D6 of F5-26 (SchedMD, Slurm "Topology Guide"; Kubernetes documentation "Control Topology Management Policies on a node" and "Resource Bin Packing" (tier 2)); R1 of F5-26 (lab run of Listing 1 on gpupack.in: F5-26/gpupack.out, gpupack.log (g++ 13.3.0, ASan and UBSan, exit code 0)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: starting all the parts of a parallel job at the same time, or none of them.
analogy: the cake's layers bake together or not at all.
precise: allocating and starting all processes of a parallel job simultaneously (all-or-nothing); without it, parts of several jobs can hold resources while waiting for their other parts, wasting the resources or deadlocking.
source: D7 of F5-26 (Dror G. Feitelson, Larry Rudolph, "Gang Scheduling Performance Benefits for Fine-Grain Synchronization", Journal of Parallel and Distributed Computing, 1992 (tier 5)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: ways for several jobs to use one GPU.
analogy: splitting a big oven into fixed compartments, letting several bakers use it at once, or taking turns.
precise: multi-Instance GPU (MIG) partitions supported NVIDIA GPUs into isolated instances with their own memory and compute slices; the Multi-Process Service (MPS) lets kernels from several processes run concurrently through one server; time slicing alternates contexts on the whole GPU. They differ in isolation, in memory protection and in what the scheduler counts.
source: D3 of F5-26 (NVIDIA, "NVIDIA Multi-Instance GPU User Guide" (tier 1–2, vendor documentation)); D4 of F5-26 (NVIDIA, "Multi-Process Service" documentation (tier 1–2, vendor documentation)); L1 of F5-26 (CUDA 12.0 headers in the build container (tier 4, opened): cuda.h line 240 (CUDA_VERSION 12000) and lines 4250–4251 (MIG UUID of "the subscribed MIG compute instance"); cuda_runtime_api.h lines 4936–4937 (CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES "is recommended to restrict CUDA to only use those GPUs that have peer-to-peer support") and 4946–4947 (environment variables "described in the CUDA programming guide"), line 1409 (cudaGetDeviceCount); driver_types.h line 545 (cudaErrorNoDevice = 100), lines 955–978 (MPS error codes)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: google's cluster manager, which runs most of the company's programs on shared clusters; the paper about it shaped Kubernetes.
analogy: lucía's rules for the shared kitchens.
precise: a cluster management system that admits, schedules, starts, restarts and monitors both long-running services and batch jobs on shared cells of machines, described in Verma et al., EuroSys 2015.
source: D1 of F5-27 (Abhishek Verma, Luis Pedrosa, Madhukar Korupolu, David Oppenheimer, Eric Tune, John Wilkes, "Large-scale cluster management at Google with Borg", Proceedings of the European Conference on Computer Systems (EuroSys), 2015 (tier 5; the course card's mapped source)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: one big shared cluster managed as a unit.
analogy: the four kitchens under one set of rules.
precise: a set of machines, within one data-centre building or cluster, managed by one Borgmaster; jobs are submitted to a cell.
source: D1 of F5-27 (Abhishek Verma, Luis Pedrosa, Madhukar Korupolu, David Oppenheimer, Eric Tune, John Wilkes, "Large-scale cluster management at Google with Borg", Proceedings of the European Conference on Computer Systems (EuroSys), 2015 (tier 5; the course card's mapped source)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the central brain of a cell, kept on several machines, and the small agent on every machine.
analogy: lucía with four deputies who keep identical notebooks; the caretaker in each kitchen.
precise: the Borgmaster is a logically centralised controller replicated over several machines, with its state stored through Paxos; one replica is elected master; a Borglet on each machine starts and stops tasks, manages local resources and reports state when polled.
source: D1 of F5-27 (Abhishek Verma, Luis Pedrosa, Madhukar Korupolu, David Oppenheimer, Eric Tune, John Wilkes, "Large-scale cluster management at Google with Borg", Proceedings of the European Conference on Computer Systems (EuroSys), 2015 (tier 5; the course card's mapped source)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a class of work, such as "production" or "batch", that decides who may interrupt whom.
analogy: café chores and hobby chores.
precise: a range of job priorities treated alike by policy; in Borg, higher-priority tasks may preempt lower-priority ones, production-band tasks do not preempt each other, and quota is granted per priority.
source: D1 of F5-27 (Abhishek Verma, Luis Pedrosa, Madhukar Korupolu, David Oppenheimer, Eric Tune, John Wilkes, "Large-scale cluster management at Google with Borg", Proceedings of the European Conference on Computer Systems (EuroSys), 2015 (tier 5; the course card's mapped source)); R1 of F5-27 (lab run of Listing 1 on borgsim.in: F5-27/borgsim.out, borgsim.log (g++ 13.3.0, ASan and UBSan, exit code 0)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: an allowance of resources per user and priority, checked when work is submitted, not when it is placed.
analogy: the yearly oven-hours allowance.
precise: a per-user, per-priority vector of resource amounts that a user may request; a job whose requests exceed the remaining quota is rejected immediately at submission (admission control), so the scheduler's queue holds only work the cell has promised to run.
source: D1 of F5-27 (Abhishek Verma, Luis Pedrosa, Madhukar Korupolu, David Oppenheimer, Eric Tune, John Wilkes, "Large-scale cluster management at Google with Borg", Proceedings of the European Conference on Computer Systems (EuroSys), 2015 (tier 5; the course card's mapped source)); R1 of F5-27 (lab run of Listing 1 on borgsim.in: F5-27/borgsim.out, borgsim.log (g++ 13.3.0, ASan and UBSan, exit code 0)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: stopping a lower-priority task to make room for a higher-priority one.
analogy: the café rush throwing out the sourdough.
precise: the eviction of running tasks chosen by priority so that a pending higher-priority task becomes feasible; the evicted tasks return to the pending queue and lose any progress not saved in a checkpoint.
source: D1 of F5-27 (Abhishek Verma, Luis Pedrosa, Madhukar Korupolu, David Oppenheimer, Eric Tune, John Wilkes, "Large-scale cluster management at Google with Borg", Proceedings of the European Conference on Computer Systems (EuroSys), 2015 (tier 5; the course card's mapped source)); R1 of F5-27 (lab run of Listing 1 on borgsim.in: F5-27/borgsim.out, borgsim.log (g++ 13.3.0, ASan and UBSan, exit code 0)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: letting low-priority work use what high-priority work reserved but is not using.
analogy: hobby bakers in the café's spare ovens, ready to leave.
precise: estimating each task's actual needs (its reservation) from observed usage, and scheduling lower-priority work against reservations instead of limits; the reclaimed capacity is revocable when the reserving task's usage grows.
source: D1 of F5-27 (Abhishek Verma, Luis Pedrosa, Madhukar Korupolu, David Oppenheimer, Eric Tune, John Wilkes, "Large-scale cluster management at Google with Borg", Proceedings of the European Conference on Computer Systems (EuroSys), 2015 (tier 5; the course card's mapped source)); R1 of F5-27 (lab run of Listing 1 on borgsim.in: F5-27/borgsim.out, borgsim.log (g++ 13.3.0, ASan and UBSan, exit code 0)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a job that never finishes because it keeps losing its turn.
analogy: the sourdough, started five times and never baked.
precise: indefinite postponement of a task's completion by the scheduling policy, for example by repeated preemption of a task whose work is lost each time.
source: R2 of F5-27 (lab run of Listing 1 on starve.in (forensic evidence): F5-27/starve.out, starve.log (same toolchain, exit code 0))
